author: Lactantius

passages.original: non uident qui deos multos esse credunt fieri posse ut aliquid diuersum uelint, ex qua re disceptatio inter eos et certamen oriatur; sicut Homerus bellantes inter se deos finxit, cum alii Troiam capi uellent, alii repugnarent.
passages.english: Those who believe that there are many gods do not see that it can happen that they want something different, and from this dispute and conflict arises among them; just as Homer invented gods warring among themselves, when some wanted Troy to be taken and others opposed it.

passages.original: Anaxagoras deum esse dicit infinitam mentem quae per se ipsam moueatur: Antisthenes multos quidem esse populares deos, unum tamen naturalem id est summae totius artificem.
passages.english: Anaxagoras says that god is an infinite mind which moves by itself; Antisthenes [says] that there are indeed many popular gods, but one natural [god], that is, the maker of the whole universe.

passages.original: Cleanthes et Anaximenes aethera esse dicunt summum deum, cui opinioni poeta noster adsensit: tum pater omnipotens fecundis imbribus aether coniugis in gremium laetae descendit et omnis magnus alit magno permixtus corpore fetus.
passages.english: Cleanthes and Anaximenes say that the aether is the supreme god, an opinion to which our poet assented: "Then the almighty father Aether descends with fertile showers into the lap of his joyful consort, and, mingled with her great body, the great one nourishes all offspring."
passages.notes: The verses are Virgil, Georgics 2.325–327.

passages.original: Nunc ad diuina testimonia transeamus. sed prius unum proferam, quod est simile diuino et ob nimiam uetustatem et quod is quem nominabo ex hominibus in deos relatus est.. apud Ciceronem U.
passages.english: Now let us pass to divine testimonies. But first I shall bring forward one that is like a divine [testimony], both because of its great antiquity and because the one whom I shall name was carried over from among men into [the number of] the gods. In Cicero ...
passages.notes: The passage breaks off after "apud Ciceronem"; the stray "U." is probably a scanning error or fragment and has not been translated.

passages.original: M. Varro, quo nemo umquam doctior ne apud Graecos quidem uixit, in libris rerum diuinarum quos ad C. Caesarem pontificem maximum scripsit, cum de quindecimuiris loqueretur, Sibyllinos libros ait non fuisse unius Sibyllae, sed appellari uno nomine Sibyllinos, quod omnes feminae uates Sibyllae sint a ueteribus nuncupatae uel ab unius Delphidis nomine uel a consiliis deorum enuntiandis. atouq enim deos, non Osouc, et consilium non βουλήν, sed βούλλαν appellabant Aeolico genere sermonis.
passages.english: Marcus Varro, than whom no one more learned ever lived, not even among the Greeks, in the books of Divine Antiquities which he wrote to Gaius Caesar, the pontifex maximus, when he was speaking about the Fifteen Men (quindecimviri), says that the Sibylline books were not of one Sibyl, but are called by one name "Sibylline" because all women prophets were named Sibyls by the ancients, either from the name of one, the Delphic [Sibyl], or from their announcing the counsels of the gods. For in the Aeolic form of speech they called the gods not theous but sious, and counsel not boulē but boulla.
passages.notes: The Greek is garbled in the scan ("atouq", "Osouc"); read as σιούς and θεούς, as the following context (θεοβούλην) requires.

passages.original: si eos multitudo delectat, non duodecim dicimus aut trecentos sexaginta quinque ut Orpheus, sed innumerabiles esse. arguimus errores eorum in diuersum, qui tam paucos putant. sciant tamen quo nomine appellari debeant, ne uiolent uerum deum, cuius nomen exponunt, dum pluribus tribuunt.
passages.english: If a multitude pleases them, we do not say there are twelve, or three hundred and sixty-five as Orpheus [does], but innumerable. We refute their errors in the opposite direction, who think there are so few. Let them know, however, by what name they ought to be called, so that they do not violate the true God, whose name they expound while they attribute it to many.

passages.original: His igitur tot ac tantis testibus conprobatur unius dei potestate ac prouidentia mundum gubernari, cuius uim maiestatemque tantam esse dicit in Timaeo Plato, ut eam neque mente concipere neque uerbis enarrare quisquam possit ob) nimiam et inaestimabilem potestatem.
passages.english: By so many and such great witnesses, therefore, it is proved that the world is governed by the power and providence of one God, whose force and majesty Plato says in the Timaeus is so great that no one can either conceive it in mind or set it out in words, because of his excessive and inestimable power.

passages.original: unde mihi de tanta maiestate saepius cogitanti qui deos colunt interdum uideri solent tam caeci, tam incogitabiles, tam excordes, tam non multum a mutis animalibus differentes, qui credant eos qui geniti sint maris ac feminae coitu aliquid maiestatis diuinaeque uirtutis habere potuisse, cum Sibylla Erythraea dicat: ouοὐ δύνατ\' ἀνδρὸς ἑϰ μηρῶν μήτρας τε θεὸς τετυπωμένος εἶναι.
passages.english: Hence, when I think more often about such great majesty, those who worship the gods sometimes seem to me so blind, so thoughtless, so senseless, so little different from dumb animals, since they believe that those who were begotten by the intercourse of male and female could have had anything of majesty and divine power, when the Erythraean Sibyl says: "A god cannot be fashioned from the loins of a man and a womb."
passages.notes: Stray "ou" before the Greek omitted as a scanning error.

passages.original: sed tanti erat uoluptas. \'quid tu?\' inquiet aliquis \'poetisne credendum putas?\' quidni putem? non enim Lucilius ista narrat aut Lucianus, qui diis et hominibus non pepercit, set ii potissimum, qui deorum laudes canebant.
passages.english: But pleasure was worth so much. "What about you?" someone will say. "Do you think the poets are to be believed?" Why should I not think so? For it is not Lucilius who tells these things, or Lucian, who spared neither gods nor men, but above all those who sang the praises of the gods.

passages.original: hunc Tarquitius de inlustribus uiris disserens ait incertis parentibus natum, expositum et a uenatoribus inuentum, canino lacte nutritum, Chironi traditum didicisse medicinam; fuisse autem Messenium, sed Epidauri moratum. Tullius etiam Cynosuris ait sepultum.
passages.english: Tarquitius, discussing illustrious men, says that he was born of uncertain parents, exposed, and found by hunters, nourished on dog's milk, handed over to Chiron, and learned medicine; and that he was a Messenian, but lived at Epidaurus. Tullius also says he was buried at Cynosurae.
passages.notes: "He" is Aesculapius, named in the preceding text (not supplied).

passages.original: \'I seu humanam? Iouem enim Iunonemque a iuuando esse dictos Cicero interpretatur et Iuppiter quasi iuuans pater dicitur: quod nomen in deum minime congruit, quia iuuare hominis est opis aliquid conferentis in eum qui sit alienus, et exigui beneficii.
passages.english: ... or human? For Cicero interprets Jupiter and Juno as named from "helping" (iuvare), and Jupiter is called, as it were, "helping father" (iuvans pater): a name which is not at all fitting for a god, because to help belongs to a man who confers some aid on another who is not his own, and [it is a matter] of slight benefit.
passages.notes: The opening "'I seu humanam?" is a fragment of a preceding sentence and partly corrupt; only "or human?" is rendered.

passages.original: qui quomodo argumentari potuerit, ostendi. nunc dicam quomodo, ubi, a quo sit hoc factum: non enim Saturnus hoc, sed Iuppiter fecit. in Sacra Historia sic Ennius tradit:
passages.english: How he was able to argue this, I have shown. Now I will say how, where, and by whom this was done: for it was not Saturn but Jupiter who did it. In the Sacred History Ennius relates it thus:

passages.original: Caesar quoque in Arato refert Aglaosthenen dicere, Iouem cum ex insula Naxo aduersus Titanas proficisceretur et sacrificium faceret in litore, aquilam ei in auspicium aduolasse, quam uictor bono omine acceptam tutelae suae subiugarit.
passages.english: Caesar too, in his Aratus, reports that Aglaosthenes says that when Jupiter was setting out from the island of Naxos against the Titans and was sacrificing on the shore, an eagle flew to him as an omen, which, as victor, having received it as a good omen, he placed under his protection.
passages.notes: "Caesar" is Germanicus, translator of Aratus. "Subiugarit" is odd; the sense is that he took the eagle into his tutelage.

passages.original: sed homines respectu elementi quod dicitur caelum totam fabulam explodunt tamquam ineptissime fictam, quam tamen Stoici ut solent ad rationem physicam conantur traducere. quorum sententiam Cicero de natura deorum disserens posuit.
passages.english: But people, having regard to the element that is called heaven, hoot the whole story off the stage as most absurdly invented; yet the Stoics, as is their habit, try to convert it into a physical explanation. Cicero, discussing the nature of the gods, set out their view.

passages.original: item noster Maro: aureus hanc uitam in terris Saturnus agebat. et alio loco:aurea quae perhibent illo sub rege fuere saecula: sic placida populos in pace regebat.
passages.english: Likewise our own Maro: "Golden Saturn led this life on earth." And in another place: "The ages they call golden were under that king: so did he rule the peoples in calm peace."
passages.notes: Maro is Virgil (Georgics 2.538; Aeneid 8.324–325).

passages.original: Ennius quidem in Euhemero non primum dicit regnasse Saturnum, sed Uranum patrem. initio inquit primus in terris imperium summum Caelus habuit. is id regnum uua cum fratribus suis sibi instituit atque parauit.
passages.english: Ennius indeed, in the Euhemerus, says that Saturn did not reign first, but his father Uranus. "In the beginning," he says, "Caelus first held supreme power on earth. He established and prepared that kingdom for himself together with his brothers."
passages.notes: 'uua' is read as 'una' (together), an evident scanning error.

passages.original: haec historia quam uera sit, docet Sibylla Erythraea eadem fere dicens, nisi quod in paucis quae ad rem non attinent discrepat.
passages.english: How true this history is, the Erythraean Sibyl shows, saying almost the same things, except that she differs in a few points that do not bear on the matter.

passages.original: quod Cicero de natura deorum docet dicens: suscepit autem uita hominum consuetudoque communis, ut beneficiis excellentis uiros in caelum fama ac uoluntate tollerent. hinc Hercules, hinc Castor, hinc Pollux, hinc Aesculapius, hinc Liber.
passages.english: This Cicero teaches in On the Nature of the Gods, saying: "But the life of men and common custom have adopted [the practice] of raising to heaven, by fame and goodwill, men outstanding for their benefactions. Hence Hercules, hence Castor, hence Pollux, hence Aesculapius, hence Liber."

passages.original: an potest aliquis dubitare, quomodo religiones deorum sint institutae, cum apud Maronem legat Aeneae uerba sociis imperantis: nunc pateras libate Ioui precibusque uocate Anchisen genitorem —? cui non tantum immortalitatem, uerum etiam uentorum tribuit potestatem: poscamus uentos, atque haec me sacra quotannis urbe uelit posita templis sibi ferre dicatis.
passages.english: Or can anyone doubt how the cults of the gods were instituted, when he reads in Maro the words of Aeneas commanding his companions: "Now pour libations from your bowls to Jupiter, and call with prayers on Anchises my father"? To him he attributes not only immortality but also power over the winds: "Let us ask for winds, and may he wish me, once the city is founded, to bring him these rites every year in temples dedicated to him."
passages.notes: Maro is Virgil; the quotations are from the Aeneid.

passages.original: ob hanc uanitatem Sibylla sic eos increpat: Ἑλλὰς δὴ, τί πέποιθας ἐπ᾽ ἀνδράσιν ἡγεμόνεσσι;πρὸς τί δὲ δῶρα μάταια καταφθιμένοις πορίζεις;θύεις εἰδώλοις; τίς σοι πλάνον ἐν φρεσὶ θῆκεν ταῦτα τελεῖν προλιπόντα θεοῦ μεγάλοιο πρόσωπον.
passages.english: On account of this folly the Sibyl rebukes them thus: "Greece, why do you trust in men as rulers? Why do you offer vain gifts to the dead? Do you sacrifice to idols? Who put error in your mind, that you should do these things, abandoning the face of the great God?"
passages.notes: The quotation is in Greek verse in the original.

passages.original: fortasse dicat aliquis prae nimio luctu delirasse Ciceronem. atquin illa omnis oratio et doctrina et exemplis et ipso loquendi genere perfecta non aegri, sed constantis animi ac iudicii fuit et haec ipsa sententia nullum praefert indicium doloris.
passages.english: Perhaps someone may say that Cicero raved from excessive grief. And yet that whole speech, perfect in learning, in examples and in its very style of speaking, was [the product] of a mind and judgement not sick but steady, and this very statement shows no sign of grief.

passages.original: suis in rem publicam meritis etiam defuncti hominis honore caruisset, et quidem consilio Pisonis soceri et Lucii Caesaris propinqui, qui uetabant funus ei fieri, et Dolabellae consulis, qui columnam in foro id est tumulum eius euertit ac forum expiauit. nam Romulum desiderio suis fuisse declarat Ennius, apud quem populus amissum regem dolens haec loquitur:
passages.english: for his services to the state he would have been deprived even of the honour due to a dead man, and that indeed by the counsel of Piso his father-in-law and of Lucius Caesar his kinsman, who forbade a funeral to be held for him, and of Dolabella the consul, who overturned the column in the forum, that is, his tomb, and purified the forum. For Ennius declares that Romulus was missed by his own people; in his work the people, grieving for the lost king, say these words:
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the subject (Julius Caesar) is implied from the preceding text.

passages.original: magnum hoc opus et homine dignum, religionum animos nodis exsoluere pergo, ut ait Lucretius, qui quidem hoc efficere non poterat, quia nihil ueri adferebat. nostrum est hoc officium, qui et uerum deum adserimus et falsos refutamus.
passages.english: "A great work, and worthy of a man: I go on to free minds from the knots of religion," as Lucretius says, who indeed could not accomplish this, because he brought nothing true. This duty is ours, who both assert the true God and refute the false ones.

passages.original: si domos habent, consequens est ut et urbes habeant, et quidem auctore Nasone, qui ait: plebs habitat diuersa locis, a fronte potentes caelicolae clarique suos posuere penates. si habent urbes, et agros igitur habebunt.
passages.english: If they have houses, it follows that they also have cities, and indeed on the authority of Naso, who says: "The common folk live in various places; in front, the powerful and illustrious heaven-dwellers have set their household gods." If they have cities, then they will also have fields.
passages.notes: Naso is Ovid (Metamorphoses).

passages.original: insulam Samum scribit Varro prius Partheniam nominatam, quod ibi Iuno adoleuerit ibique etiam Ioui nupserit. itaque nobilissimum et antiquissimum templum eius est Sami et simulacrum in habitu nubentis figuratum et sacra eius anniuersaria nuptiarum ritu celebrantur.
passages.english: Varro writes that the island of Samos was formerly called Parthenia, because Juno grew up there and there also married Jupiter. Therefore her most famous and most ancient temple is at Samos, and [there is] a statue shaped in the dress of a bride, and her yearly rites are celebrated in the manner of a wedding.

passages.original: aput Ennium sic loquitur Africanus: 25 si fas endo plagas caelestum ascendere cuiquam est, mi soli caeli maxima porta patet, scilicet quia magnam partem generis humani extinxit ac perdidit.
passages.english: In Ennius Africanus speaks thus: "If it is lawful for anyone to ascend into the regions of the heavenly ones, for me alone the greatest gate of heaven stands open" — evidently because he destroyed and ruined a great part of the human race.
passages.notes: The '25' before the verse is a line number from the printed edition and has been omitted.

passages.original: nec hanc solam Romani meretricem colunt, sed Faulam quoque, quam Herculis scortum fuisse Verrius scribit. iam quanta ista inmortalitas putanda est, quam etiam meretrices adsecuntur?
passages.english: Nor do the Romans worship only this prostitute, but also Faula, who Verrius writes was the harlot of Hercules. Now how great must this immortality be thought, which even prostitutes attain?

passages.original: magnum Cicero audaxque consilium suscepisse Graeciam dicit, quod Cupidinum et Amorum simulacra in gymnasiis consecrasset: adulatus est uidelicet Attico et inrisit hominem familiarem.
passages.english: Cicero says that Greece undertook a great and bold plan in consecrating images of the Cupids and Loves in the gymnasia: evidently he was flattering Atticus and mocking his intimate friend.

passages.original: uerum id genus sacrificii ab Hercule, cum ex Hispania rediret, dicitur esse sublatum, ritu tamen permanente ut pro ueris hominibus imagines iacerentur e scirpo, ut Ouidius in Fastis docet: donec in haec uenit Tirynthius arua, quotannis tristia Leucadio sacra peracta modo. illum stramineos in aquam misisse Quirites, Herculis exemplo corpora falsa iaci.
passages.english: But that kind of sacrifice is said to have been abolished by Hercules when he was returning from Spain, though the rite remained that, instead of real men, figures made of rushes were thrown [into the water], as Ovid teaches in the Fasti: "Until the Tirynthian came into these fields, grim rites were performed every year in the Leucadian manner. He threw men of straw into the water; [now], following Hercules' example, false bodies are thrown."
passages.notes: The last line of the Ovid quotation is elliptical; 'Quirites' (Romans) seems to be the subject of the throwing in the original, i.e. the Romans throw straw figures by Hercules' example; the text may be compressed or corrupt.

passages.original: sectis namque umeris et utraque manu destrictos gladios exerentes currunt ecferuntur insaniunt. optime igitur Quintilianus in Fanatico istud inquit si deus cogit, iratus est.
passages.english: For with their shoulders cut, and brandishing drawn swords in each hand, they run, they are carried away, they rave. So Quintilian put it excellently in the *Fanaticus*: "If a god compels this, he is angry."
passages.notes: "Fanaticus" is a lost declamation attributed to Quintilian.

passages.original: nam primo sacerdotes eius deglabrato corpore pectora sua tundunt lamentantur, sicut ipsa cum perdidit fecerat; deinde puer producitur quasi inuentus et in laetitiam luctus ille mutatur. ideo Lucanus:numquamque satis quaesitus Osiris.
passages.english: For first her priests, their bodies shaved smooth, beat their breasts and lament, as she herself had done when she lost [him]; then the boy is brought forward as if found, and that mourning is turned into joy. Hence Lucan: "and Osiris, never sought enough."

passages.original: sed et matris eius mysterium idem continet; quod Ouidius exponit in Fastis: ardua iam dudum resonat tinnitibus Ide, tutus ut infanti uagiat ore puer. pars clipeos sudibus, galeas pars tundit inanes,hoc Curetes habent, hoc Corybantes opus. res latuit priscique manent imitamina facti, aera deae comites raucaque terga mouent. cymbala pro galeis, pro scutis tympana pulsant., tibia dat Phrygios ut dedit ante modos.
passages.english:
But the mystery of his mother also contains the same [thing]; Ovid sets it out in the *Fasti*:
Long since has lofty Ida rung with clashing,
so that the boy may wail safely with infant mouth.
Some beat shields with stakes, some beat empty helmets;
the Curetes have this task, the Corybantes this.
The matter stayed hidden, and imitations of the ancient deed remain:
the goddess's companions shake bronzes and hoarse hides.
They strike cymbals instead of helmets, drums instead of shields;
the pipe gives Phrygian measures, as it gave before.
passages.notes: "Mother" here is presumably Cybele/Rhea, mother of Jupiter; the preceding context is missing.

passages.original: non ergo ille Funus, sed plane furiosus fuit, qui praeturam hoc ministerio se putauit ornare. merito igitur, cum haec a uiris non inperitis ac rudibus fiant, Lucretius exclamat: o stultas hominum mentes, o pectora caeca! qualibus in tenebris uitae quantisque periclis degitur hoc aeui quodcumque est!
passages.english: So that man was not Funus but plainly furious, who thought he was adorning his praetorship with this service. Rightly, then, since these things are done by men who are not ignorant and uncouth, Lucretius exclaims: "O foolish minds of men, O blind hearts! In what darkness of life and in how great dangers is this span of time, whatever it is, spent!"
passages.notes: A pun on the name Funus ("funeral") and furiosus ("mad"); the person referred to cannot be identified from the passage alone.

passages.original: eandem Varro scribit tantae pudicitiae fuisse, ut nemo illam quoad uixerit praeter suum uirum mas uiderit nec nomen eius audierit.
passages.english: Varro writes that this same woman was of such great chastity that, as long as she lived, no male except her own husband saw her or heard her name.

passages.original: recte igitur Seneca in libris moralibus simulacra inquit deorum uenerantur, illis supplicant genu posito, illa adorant, illis per totum adsident diem aut adstant, illis stipem iaciunt, uictimas caedunt: et cum haec tanto opere suspiciant, fabros qui illa fecere contemnunt.
passages.english: Rightly, then, Seneca says in his books on morals: "They venerate images of the gods, they supplicate them on bended knee, they worship them, they sit or stand beside them all day long, they toss coins to them, they slaughter victims; and while they look up to these things so greatly, they despise the craftsmen who made them."

passages.original: Quid igitur maiestatis possunt habere simulacra, quae fuerunt in homunculi potestate uel ut aliud fierent uel ut omnino ne fierent? idcirco aput Horatium Priapus ita loquitur: olim truncus eram ficulnus, inutile lignum cam faber incertus scamnum faceretne Priapum,maluit esse deum. deus inde ego, furum auiumque maxima formido.
passages.english: What majesty, then, can images have which were in the power of a little man either to become something else or not to come into being at all? That is why in Horace Priapus speaks thus: "Once I was a fig-wood trunk, useless timber, when the craftsman, uncertain whether to make a stool or Priapus, preferred that I be a god. A god, then, I am, the greatest terror of thieves and birds."
passages.notes: "cam" read as "cum" (scanning error).

passages.original: sed quid mirum si aut barhari aut inperiti homines errant, cum etiam philosophi Stoicae disciplinae in eadem sint opinione, ut omnia caelestia quae mouentur in deorum numero habenda esse censeant? siquidem Lucilius Stoicus aput Ciceronem sic loquitur:
passages.english: But what wonder is it if barbarians or ignorant men err, when even philosophers of the Stoic school hold the same opinion, judging that all the heavenly things that move are to be counted among the gods? Indeed Lucilius the Stoic speaks thus in Cicero:
passages.notes: 'barhari' read as 'barbari'.

passages.original: denique aput Ciceronem sic dicit Cotta Lucilio: habes, Balbe, quid Cotta, quid pontifex sentiat. fac nunc ego intellegam quid tu sentias: a te enim philosopho rationem religionis accipere debeo, maioribus autem nostris etiam nulla ratione reddita. credere.
passages.english: Finally, in Cicero, Cotta speaks thus to Lucilius: "You have, Balbus, what Cotta thinks, what the pontiff thinks. Now let me understand what you think: for from you, a philosopher, I ought to receive a reasoned account of religion, but our ancestors I ought to believe even when no reason is given."
passages.notes: The full stop before "credere" is a scanning or punctuation error; "credere" completes the sentence ("debeo ... credere").

passages.original: ita conflauit ex his omnibus populum legitque in senatum eos qui aetate anteibant et patres appellauit, quorum consilio gereret omnia. de quo senatu Propertius elegiarum scriptor haec loquitur: bucina cogebat priscos ad uerba Quirites,centum illi in prato saepe senatus erat. curia, praetexto nunc quae nitet alta senatu, pellitos habuit, rustica corda, patres.
passages.english:
Thus he formed a people out of all these, and chose into the senate those who were foremost in age and called them fathers, by whose counsel he would manage everything. Of this senate Propertius, the writer of elegies, says this:
The trumpet used to summon the ancient Quirites to speeches;
those hundred in a meadow were often the senate.
The senate house, which now gleams on high with its purple-bordered senate,
once held fathers clad in skins, rustic hearts.

passages.original: nam Cicero de natura deorum disputans ait sic: primum igitur non est proba-. bile eam materiam rerum unde omnia. orta. sunt esse diuina prouidentia effectam, sed et habere etha-buisse uim et naturam suam.
passages.english: For Cicero, discussing the nature of the gods, speaks thus: "First, then, it is not probable that the matter of things, from which all things have arisen, was made by divine providence, but rather that it has and has had a force and nature of its own."
passages.notes: Scanning debris ("proba-.", "etha-buisse") read as "probabile" and "et habuisse".

passages.original: nam diuina prouidentia efFectum esse mundum, ut taceam de Trismegisto qui hoc praedicat, taceam de carminibus Sibyllarum quae idem nuntiant, taceam de prophetis qui opus mundi et opificium dei uno spiritu et pari uoce testantur, etiam inter philosophos paene uniuersos conuenit; id enim Pythagorei Stoici Peripatetici, quae sunt principales omnium disciplinae.
passages.english: For that the world was made by divine providence—to say nothing of Trismegistus, who proclaims this, nothing of the songs of the Sibyls, which announce the same, nothing of the prophets, who testify with one spirit and a like voice to the work of the world and the craftsmanship of God—is agreed even among nearly all the philosophers; for this [is held by] the Pythagoreans, Stoics, Peripatetics, which are the chief schools of all.
passages.notes: The last clause lacks a verb (e.g. "hold"); the sentence may be incomplete in the text.

passages.original: nam sicut sol, qui oritur in diem, licet sit unus, unde solem esse appellatum Cicero uult uideri, quod obscuratis sideribus solus appareat, tamen quia uerum ac perfectae plenitudinis lumen est et calore potentissimo et fulgore clarissimo inlustrat omnia., ita in deo, licet sit unus, et maiestas et uirtus et claritudo perfecta est.
passages.english: For just as the sun, which rises for the day, though it is one—whence Cicero would have it seem that it was called sol, because when the stars are darkened it alone (solus) appears—nevertheless, because it is true light of perfect fullness, illuminates all things with most powerful heat and most brilliant radiance, so in God, though he is one, majesty and power and splendour are perfect.

passages.original: Hera,clitus ex igni nata esse dixit omnia, Thales ex aqua. uterque uidit aliquid, sed errauit tamen uterque, quod alterutrum si solum fuisset, neque aqua nasci posset ex igni neque rursus ignis ex aqua: sed est uerius simul ex utroque permixto cuncta generari.
passages.english: Heraclitus said that all things were born from fire, Thales from water. Each of them saw something, but each nevertheless went wrong, because if either one alone had existed, neither could water be born from fire, nor again fire from water; but it is truer that all things are generated at once from both mixed together.
passages.notes: 'Hera,clitus' is a scanning error for 'Heraclitus'.

passages.original: denique Plato humanam formam θεοειδῆ esse ait, et Sibylla quae dicit: είϰών ὲστ\' ᾰνθρωπος ἐμὴ λόγον ὀρθὸν ἔχουσα.
passages.english: Finally Plato says that the human form is *theoeidēs* [godlike], and [so does] the Sibyl, who says: "Man is my image, possessing right reason."

passages.original: Aiunt certis conuersionibus caeli et astrorum motibus maturitatem quandam extitisse animalium serendorum, itaque terram nouam semen genitale retinentem folliculos ex se quosdam in uterorum similitudinem protulisse — de quibus Lucretius: crescebant uteri terram radicibus apti — eosque cum maturuissent, natura cogente ruptos animalia tenera profudisse.
passages.english: They say that through certain revolutions of the heaven and movements of the stars there arose a kind of ripeness for the begetting of animals, and so the new earth, holding the generative seed, brought forth from itself certain sacs in the likeness of wombs (of which Lucretius [says]: "wombs grew, fastened to the earth by roots"), and that these, when they had ripened, burst under the compulsion of nature and poured out tender animals.

passages.original: sed tamen diuinis opus est testimoniis, ne minus humana sufficiant. Sibylla hominem dei opus esse testatur: ὃς μόνος ἐστὶ θεὸς ϰτίστης ὰϰράτητος ύπάρχων αὐτὸς δ\' ἐστήριξε τύπον μορϕῆς μερόπων τε -αὐτὸς ἕμιξε ϕύσιν πάντων, γενέτης βιότοιο.
passages.english: But nevertheless there is need of divine testimonies, lest human ones be insufficient. The Sibyl testifies that man is the work of God: "He who alone is God, the creator, being unconquered, he himself fixed the pattern of the form of mortals, he himself mixed the nature of all things, the begetter of life."

passages.original: Empedocles, quem nescias utrumne inter poetas an inter philosophos numeres, quia de rerum natura uersibus scripsit ut aput Romanos Lucretius et Varro, quattuor elementa constituit, ignem aerem aquam terram, fortasse Trismegistum secutus, qui nostra, corpora ei his quattuor elementis constituta. esse dixit a deo:
passages.english: Empedocles, whom you could not tell whether to count among the poets or among the philosophers, because he wrote on the nature of things in verse, as Lucretius and Varro did among the Romans, established four elements, fire, air, water, earth, perhaps following Trismegistus, who said that our bodies were constituted by God from these four elements:
passages.notes: "ei his" read as "ex his"; stray punctuation in the edition ignored.

passages.original: quod quidem non fugit hominem nequam Sallustium, qui ait: sed nostra omnis uis in a.nimo et corpore sita, est: animi imperio, corporis seruitio magis utimur.
passages.english: This indeed did not escape that worthless man Sallust, who says: "But all our power is located in mind and body: we use the mind more for command, the body for service."
passages.notes: 'a.nimo' and 'sita, est' are scanning errors for 'animo' and 'sita est'.

passages.original: tum deus sententia in peccatores data eiecit hominem de Paradiso, ut uictum sibi labore conquireret, ipsumque Paradisum igni circumuallauit, ne homo posset accedere, donec summum iudicium faciat in terra et iustos uiros cultores suos in eundem locum reuocet morte sublata, sicut sacrae uoces docent et Sibylla Erythraea, cum dicit: οἱ δὲ θεὸν τιμῶντες ἀληθινὸν ἀέναόν τε ζωὴν κληρονομοῦσι, τὸν αἰῶνος χρόνον αὐτοὶ οἰκοῦντες Παράδεισον ὁμῶς, ὲριθηλέα κῆπον. aerum haec quoniam extrema sunt, in extrema.
passages.english: Then God, having passed sentence on the sinners, cast man out of Paradise, so that he might obtain his food for himself by labour, and he surrounded Paradise itself with a wall of fire, so that man could not approach, until he holds the supreme judgement on earth and calls back just men, his worshippers, to that same place, with death abolished, as the sacred words teach and [also] the Erythraean Sibyl, when she says: "But those who honour the true and everlasting God inherit life, they themselves dwelling for the time of the age likewise in Paradise, the flourishing garden." But since these things are the last, in the last
passages.notes: 'aerum' is evidently a scanning error for 'uerum' ('but'). The final sentence is incomplete and continues in the next unit.

passages.original: operis huius parte tractabimus: nunc ea quae prima sunt explicemus. mors itaque secuta est hominem secundum dei sententiam, quod etiam Sibylla in carmine suo docet dicens: ὰνθρωπον πλασθέντα θεοῦ παλάμαις άγίαισιν,ὃν ἀ ὲπλάνησεν ὅϕις δολίως ἐπὶ μοῖραν ἀνελθεῖν τοῦ θανάτου γνῶσιν τε λαβεῖν ἀγαθοῦ τε κακοῦ τε.
passages.english: part of this work we shall treat [them]; now let us explain the things which are first. Death therefore followed man according to the sentence of God, which the Sibyl also teaches in her song, saying: "Man, formed by the holy hands of God, whom the serpent deceitfully led astray to come to the fate of death and to receive knowledge of good and evil."
passages.notes: The sentence continues from the previous unit. The Greek has a stray 'ἀ' after 'ὃν', probably a scanning error, and it is omitted.

passages.original: unde illum Trismegistus daemonia-rchen uocat. daemonas autem grammatici dictos aiunt quasi δαή- μονας, id est peritos ac rerum scios: hos enim putant deos esse. sciunt illi quidem futura multa, sed non omnia, quippe quibus penitus consilium dei scire non liceat, et ideo solent responsa in ambiguos exitus temperare.
passages.english: Hence Trismegistus calls him *daimoniarchēs* [ruler of demons]. And the grammarians say that *daemones* [demons] are so called as if *daēmones*, that is, skilled and knowing of things; for they think these are gods. They do indeed know many future things, but not all, since they are not permitted to know the counsel of God thoroughly, and therefore they are accustomed to tune their responses toward ambiguous outcomes.
passages.notes: 'daemonia-rchen' and 'δαή- μονας' are split words from the scan.

passages.original: eos poetae et sciunt esse daemonas et locuntur. Hesiodus ita tradit: τοὶ μὲν δαίμονές εἰσι Διὸς μεγάλου διὰ βουλὰς ἐσθλοί, ἐπιχθόνιοι, ϕύλαϰες θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων.
passages.english: The poets both know that these are demons and speak [of them so]. Hesiod relates thus: "They are *daimones* [spirits] through the plans of great Zeus, good, upon the earth, guardians of mortal men."

passages.original: uterque uero daemonas esse adfirmat inimicos et uexatores hominum, quos ideo Trismegistus ἀγγέλους πονηρούς appellat: adeo non ignorauit ex caelestibus deprauatos terrenos esse coepisse.
passages.english: Both, indeed, affirm that demons are enemies and tormentors of men, whom Trismegistus for that reason calls "evil angels": so far was he from being unaware that, having been corrupted from heavenly beings, they had begun to be earthly.
passages.notes: 'Both' (uterque) refers to persons named before this passage, which is not given.

passages.original: Eorum inuenta sunt astrologia et haruspicina et auguratio et ipsa quae dicuntur oracula et necromantia. et ars magica et quidquid praeterea malorum exercent homines uel palam uel occulte: quae omnia per se falsa sunt, ut Sibylla Erythraea testatur: έπεὶ πλάνα πάντα τάδ\' έστιν,ὅσσαπερ ἄϕρονες ἄνδρες έρευνῶσιν ϰατὰ ήμαρ.
passages.english: Their inventions are astrology, haruspicy, augury, and the so-called oracles themselves, and necromancy, and the magic art, and whatever other evils besides people practise, whether openly or in secret: all of which are false in themselves, as the Erythraean Sibyl testifies: "since all these things are deceptions, which foolish men search into day by day."
passages.notes: The Sibyl's line is quoted in Greek in the original.

passages.original: quotiens autem pericula impendent, ob aliquam se ineptam et leuem causam profitentur iratos, sicut Iuno Varroni, quod formonsum puerum in tensa lorus ad exuuias tenendas conloca.cerat: et ob hanc causam Romanum nomen aput Cannas paene deletum est.
passages.english: But whenever dangers threaten, they declare themselves angry for some foolish and trivial reason, as Juno [was] with Varro, because he had placed a handsome boy in Jupiter's chariot to hold the spoils; and for this reason the Roman name was almost wiped out at Cannae.
passages.notes: "tensa lorus" read as "tensa Iouis" (the sacred car of Jupiter); "conloca.cerat" read as "conlocauerat". A *tensa* was the car carrying the images of the gods in processions.

passages.original: ergo si neque sciri quicquam potest, ut Socrates docuit, neque opinari oportet, ut Zenon, tota philosophia sublata est. quid quod non tantum ab his duobus euertitur qui philosophiae principes fuerunt, sed ab omnibus, ut iam uideatur iam pridem suis armis esse confecta?
passages.english: Therefore, if nothing can be known, as Socrates taught, nor ought one to hold opinions, as Zeno [taught], all philosophy is done away with. What of the fact that it is overturned not only by these two, who were the chief men of philosophy, but by all, so that it now seems to have long since been destroyed by its own weapons?

passages.original: uerum Arcesilas ignorantiae magister cum Zenoni obtrectaret principi Stoicorum, ut totam philosophiam euerteret, auctore Socrate suscepit hanc sententiam, ut adfirmaret sciri nihil posse.
passages.english: But Arcesilas, the teacher of ignorance, when he was disparaging Zeno, the chief of the Stoics, in order to overturn all philosophy, took up this view on the authority of Socrates, so as to assert that nothing can be known.

passages.original: Epicurus summum bonum in uoluptate animi esse censet, Aristippus in uoluptate corporis; Callipho et Dinomachus honestatem cum uoluptate iunxerunt. Diodorus in priuatione doloris summum bonum posuit, Hieronymus in non dolendo, Peripatetici autem in bonis animi et corporis et fortunae.
passages.english: Epicurus holds that the highest good lies in pleasure of the mind, Aristippus in pleasure of the body; Callipho and Dinomachus joined virtue with pleasure. Diodorus placed the highest good in the absence of pain, Hieronymus in not feeling pain, but the Peripatetics in the goods of the mind, of the body and of fortune.

passages.original: qua de re Ciceronis uera sententia est: ex tot inquit generibus nullum est animal praeter hominem quod habeat notitiam aliquam dei, ipsisque in hominibus nulla gens est neque tam mansueta neque tam fera, quae non etiamsi ignoret qualem haberi deum deceat, tamen habendum sciat.
passages.english: On this matter Cicero's view is true: "Of so many kinds," he says, "there is no animal except man that has any knowledge of god, and among men themselves there is no nation either so civilised or so savage that, even if it does not know what sort of god it is fitting to hold, nevertheless does not know that one must be held."

passages.original: Epicurus deum beatum et incorruptum uocat, quia sempiternus est. beatitudo enim perfecta esse debet, ut nihil sit quod eam uexare aut minuere aut inmutare possit.
passages.english: Epicurus calls god blessed and incorruptible, because he is everlasting. For blessedness must be perfect, so that there is nothing that can trouble, diminish or change it.

passages.original: tanti est, ut Anaxagorae uisum est, contemplatio caeli ac lucis ipsius, ut quascumque miserias libeat sustinere.
passages.english: So great a thing, as it seemed to Anaxagoras, is the contemplation of the sky and of light itself, that one would gladly endure any miseries whatever.

passages.original: Rectius itaque Lucretius, cum eum laudat qui sapientiam primus inuenit, sed hoc inepte, quod ab homine inuentam putauit: quasi uero illam alicubi iacentem homo ille quem laudabat inuenerit tamquam tibias ad fontem, ut poetae aiunt.
passages.english: So Lucretius [speaks] more rightly when he praises the one who first discovered wisdom, but [he speaks] foolishly in this, that he thought it was discovered by a man: as if indeed that man whom he was praising had found it lying somewhere, like the pipes by the spring, as the poets say.
passages.notes: The pipes by the spring: probably the myth of the flutes discarded by Athena and found by Marsyas.

passages.original: Nepos quoque Cornelius ad eundem Ciceronem ita scribit: tantum abest ut ego magistram putem esse uitae philosophiam beataeque uitae perfectricem, ut nullis magis existimem opus esse magistros uiuendi quam plerisque qui in ea disputanda uersantur. uideo enim magnam partem eorum qui in schola de pudore (et) continentia praecipiant argutissime, eosdem in omnium libidinum cupiditatibus uiuere.
passages.english: Cornelius Nepos also writes to the same Cicero as follows: "So far am I from thinking that philosophy is the teacher of life and the perfecter of the happy life, that I consider no one more in need of teachers of how to live than most of those who are occupied in discussing it. For I see that a great part of those who in the school give the most subtle precepts about modesty and self-restraint live, these same men, in the desires of every kind of lust."

passages.original: item Seneca in Exhortationibus plerique inquit philosophorum tales sunt, diserti in conuicium suum. quos si audias in auaritiam, in libidinem, in ambitionem perorantes, indicium professos putes: adeo redundant ad ipsos maledicta in publicum missa.
passages.english: Likewise Seneca in the Exhortations says: "Most philosophers are of this sort, eloquent to their own reproach. If you heard them haranguing against avarice, against lust, against ambition, you would think they had turned informer on themselves: so much do the reproaches they send out to the public rebound on themselves."
passages.notes: 'indicium professos': literally 'had declared an information', i.e. confessed/turned state's evidence against themselves.

passages.original: — faciet sapiens inquit idem Seneca etiam quae non. probabit, ut etiam ad maiora transitum inueniat, nec relinquet mores bonos, sed tempori aptabit, et quibus alii utuntur in gloriam aut uoluptatem, utetur agendae rei causa.
passages.english: "The wise man," says the same Seneca, "will also do things he does not approve, so that he may find a passage even to greater things; nor will he abandon good morals, but will adapt them to the occasion, and the things which others use for glory or pleasure he will use for the sake of getting the business done."
passages.notes: Scanning: 'non. probabit' read as 'non probabit'.

passages.original: quando inquit philosophi esse coeperunt? Thales ut opinor primus. recens haec quidem aetas: ubi ergo aput antiquiores latuit amor iste inuestigandae ueritatis? idem Lucretius ait:
passages.english: "When," he says, "did philosophers begin to exist? Thales, I think, was first. This is indeed a recent age: where, then, among the more ancient men did this love of investigating truth lie hidden?" The same Lucretius says:
passages.notes: The quotation following 'Lucretius says' is not included in the passage.

passages.original: et Seneca non sunt inquit mille anni, ex quo initia sapientiae mota sunt. multis igitur saeculis humanum genus sine ratione uixit: quod inridens Persius postquam inquit sapere urbi cum pipere et palmis uenit, tamquam sapientia cum saporis mercibus fuerit inuecta.
passages.english: And Seneca says: "It is not a thousand years since the beginnings of wisdom were set in motion." For many ages, therefore, the human race lived without reason: which Persius mocks, saying "after wisdom came to the City along with pepper and dates," as if wisdom had been imported along with goods for flavouring.
passages.notes: Wordplay between 'sapere' (be wise) and 'sapor' (flavour) is lost in English.

passages.original: quod Lucretius queritur, cum dicit de deo: tum fulmina mittat et aedis ipse suas disturbet et in deserta recedens saeuiat exercens telum, quod saepe nocentes praeterit exanimatque indignos inque merentes.
passages.english: This is what Lucretius complains of when he says of god: "then he should hurl thunderbolts, and himself wreck his own temples, and, withdrawing into the wilderness, rage as he plies his weapon, which often passes by the guilty and strikes dead the undeserving and the blameless."
passages.notes: Verse quotation (Lucretius 2.1101–1104) rendered as prose to match the single-paragraph format. The final phrase "inque merentes" is taken as "immerentes" (undeserving).

passages.original: homines autem ingeniosi quid de hoc existimauerint, ex dicto Ciceronis apparet, qui ait diuinitus extitisse illam flammam, non quae terrestre illut domicilium Iouis deleret, sed quae sublimius magnificentiusque deposceret.
passages.english: But what men of talent thought about this appears from a saying of Cicero, who says that that flame arose by divine agency, not to destroy that earthly dwelling of Jupiter, but to demand a loftier and more magnificent one.
passages.notes: "illut" is a variant spelling of "illud".

passages.original: qua de re etiam in libris consulatus sui eadem dixit quae Lucretius: nam pater altitonans stellanti nixus Olympo ipse suas arces atque inclyta templa petiuit et Capitolinis iniecit sedibus ignes.
passages.english: On this matter he also said in the books about his consulship the same things as Lucretius: "For the high-thundering father, resting on starry Olympus, himself attacked his own citadels and famous temples, and hurled fires upon the Capitoline seats."
passages.notes: Verse quotation from Cicero's poem on his consulship, rendered as prose to match the single-paragraph format.

passages.original: non enim de Socrate hoc saltem aut Platone dicebat, qui uelut reges habentur philosophorum, sed de homine, quo sano ac uigente nullus aeger ineptius delirauit. itaque poeta inanissimus leonis laudibus murem non ornauit, sed obruit et obtriuit.
passages.english: For he was not saying this about Socrates at least, or Plato, who are regarded as kings, so to speak, of the philosophers, but about a man than whom, while he was sane and in full vigour, no sick man raved more foolishly. And so the most empty-headed poet did not adorn a mouse with the praises of a lion, but buried and crushed it.
passages.notes: The context implies Lucretius praising Epicurus.

passages.original: (minime) uero inquit; nam quod cum corpore nascitur, cum corpore intereat necesse est. iam superius dixi differre me hunc locum et operi ultimo reseruare, ut hanc Epicuri persuasionem, siue illa Democriti siue Dicaearchi fuit, et argumentis et diuinis testimoniis redarguam.
passages.english: "Not at all," he says; "for what is born with the body must perish with the body." I have already said above that I am postponing this topic and reserving it for the last part of the work, so that I may refute this belief of Epicurus, whether it belonged to Democritus or to Dicaearchus, with both arguments and divine testimonies.
passages.notes: "(minime)" is an editorial supplement. The speaker is presumably Epicurus or an Epicurean; this cannot be confirmed without context.

passages.original: archipirata quispiam uel latronum ductor si suos ad grassandum cohortetur, quo alio sermone uti potest quam ut eadem dicat quae dicit Epicurus?
passages.english: If some pirate chief or leader of brigands were urging his men on to plunder, what other language could he use than to say the same things that Epicurus says?

passages.original: multi ergo ex iis qui aeternas esse animas suspicabantur, tamquam in caelum migraturi essent, sibi ipsi manus intulerunt, ut Cleanthes, ut Chrysippus, ut Zenon, ut Empedocles, qui se in ardentis Aetnae specus intempesta nocte deiecit, ut cum repente non apparuisset, abisse ad deos crederetur, et ex Romanis Cato, qui fuit in omni sua uita Stoicae uanitatis imitator.
passages.english: Many, therefore, of those who suspected that souls are eternal laid hands on themselves, as if they were going to migrate to heaven: like Cleanthes, like Chrysippus, like Zeno, like Empedocles, who threw himself into the caverns of burning Etna in the dead of night, so that, when he had suddenly disappeared, he might be believed to have gone off to the gods; and among the Romans Cato, who throughout his whole life was an imitator of Stoic vanity.

passages.original: quod adeo uerum est, ut idem Tullius in Consolatione non easdem sedes incolere iustos atque inpios praedicauerit.
passages.english: This is so true that the same Tullius, in the Consolation, declared that the just and the impious do not inhabit the same abodes.
passages.notes: Tullius is Cicero.

passages.original: quae ut maioris sit auctoritatis, Sileno adtribuitur. Cicero in Consolatione non nasci inquit longe optimum nec in hos scopulos incidere uitae, proximum autem, si natus sis, quam primum tamquam ex incendio effugere fortunae. credidisse illum uanissimo dicto exinde apparet, quod adiecit de suo aliquid, ut ornaret.
passages.english: To give it greater authority, it is attributed to Silenus. Cicero in the Consolation says that by far the best thing is not to be born and not to run onto these rocks of life, and the next best, if you have been born, is to escape as quickly as possible, as if from a fire, from fortune. That he believed this most empty saying is evident from the fact that he added something of his own to embellish it.

passages.original: non dissimile Platonis illut est, quod aiebat se gratias agere naturae: primum quod homo natus esset potius quam mutum animal, deinde quod mas potius quam femina, quod Graecus quam barbarus, postremo quod Atheniensis et quod temporibus Socratis.
passages.english: Not unlike this is that saying of Plato, who said that he gave thanks to nature: first that he had been born a human being rather than a dumb animal, next a male rather than a female, a Greek rather than a barbarian, and finally an Athenian, and in the time of Socrates.

passages.original: fuisse Seneca inter Stoicos ait qui deliberaret, utrumne soli quoque suos populos daret: inepte scilicet, qui dubitauerit. quid enim perderet, si dedisset? sed credo calor deterrebat, ne tantam multitudinem periculo committeret, ne si aestu nimio perissent, ipsius culpa euenisse tanta calamitas diceretur.
passages.english: Seneca says that there was someone among the Stoics who deliberated whether he should give the sun too its own peoples: foolishly, of course, since he was in doubt. For what would he lose if he had granted it? But, I suppose, the heat deterred him from exposing so great a multitude to danger, lest, if they perished from excessive heat, so great a calamity should be said to have happened through his fault.
passages.notes: The sense seems to be whether to assign inhabitants to the sun; the passage lacks surrounding context. The text after the passage consists only of a stray "S".

passages.original: quae uniuersa perdiscere neque feminae possunt, quibus intra puberes annos officia mox usibus domesticis profutura discenda sunt, neque serui, quibus per eos annos uel maxime seruiendum est quibus possunt discere, neque pauperes aut opifices aut rustici, quibus in diem uictus labore quaerendus est. ob eam causam Tullius ait abhorrere a multitudine philosophiam.
passages.english: Women cannot learn all these things thoroughly, since within the years before puberty they must learn the duties that will soon be useful for domestic needs. Nor can slaves, since during the very years in which they could learn they must serve most of all. Nor can the poor, or craftsmen, or farmers, who must earn their living by daily labour. For this reason Tullius says that philosophy shrinks from the multitude.
passages.notes: Tullius is Cicero.

passages.original: Epicurus multo fortius sapiens inquit semper beatus est et uel inclusus in Phalaridis tauro hanc uocem emittet: suaue est et nihil curo. quis eum non inriserit, maxime quod homo uoluptarius personam sibi uiri fortis inposuit et quidem supra modum?
passages.english: Epicurus says much more boldly: "The wise man is always happy, and even if shut up in the bull of Phalaris he will utter these words: 'It is pleasant, and I do not care.'" Who would not laugh at him, especially because a man devoted to pleasure put on himself the mask of a brave man, and indeed beyond all measure?

passages.original: Anaxagoras pronuntiat circumfusa esse tenebris omnia; Empedocles angustas esse sensuum semitas queritur, tamquam illi ad cogita-ndum reda et quadrigis opus esset;
passages.english: Anaxagoras declares that all things are surrounded by darkness; Empedocles complains that the paths of the senses are narrow, as if he needed a carriage and a four-horse team for thinking;

passages.original: quid igitur pugnes aduersus eos homines qui suo sibi gladio pereunt? quid labores ut eos destruas, quos sua ipsos destruit atque adfligit oratio? Aristoteles inquit Cicero ueteres philosophos os accusans ait eos aut stultissimos aut gloriosissimos fuisse, qui existimauissent philosophiam suis ingeniis esse perfectam: sed se uidere, quod paucis annis magna accessio facta esset, breui tempore philosophiam plane absolutam fore.
passages.english: Why then should you fight against those men who perish by their own sword? Why should you labour to destroy those whom their own speech destroys and strikes down? "Aristotle," says Cicero, "accusing the old philosophers, says that they were either very foolish or very boastful, since they had thought that philosophy had been perfected by their own talents; but he saw that, because great progress had been made in a few years, in a short time philosophy would be entirely complete."
passages.notes: "os" before "accusans" appears to be a stray scanning fragment and has been left out.

passages.original: eundem tamen interdum naturam, interdum fortunam uocant, quod multa inquit idem Cicero efficiat inopinata nobis propter obscuritatem ignorationemque causarum. cum igitur causas ignorent propter quas fiat aliquid, et ipsum qui faciat ignorent necesse est.
passages.english: Yet they call the same [being] sometimes nature, sometimes fortune, "because," as the same Cicero says, "it brings about many things unexpected by us, owing to the obscurity of causes and our ignorance of them." Since, then, they do not know the causes on account of which anything happens, they must also be ignorant of the one who makes it happen.

passages.original: cui opinioni et Vergilius adsentit, qui fortunam omnipotentem uocat, et historicus, qui ait: sed profecto fortuna in omni re dominatur. quid ergo ceteris diis loci superest?
passages.english: Virgil too agrees with this opinion, calling fortune all-powerful, and so does the historian, who says: "But assuredly fortune holds sway in every matter." What room, then, is left for the other gods?
passages.notes: The historian is evidently Sallust (Catiline 8.1).

passages.original: huius itaque peruersae potestatis cum uim sentirent uirtuti repugnantem, nomen ignorarent, fortunae sibi uocabulum inane finxerunt: quod quam longe a sapientia sit remotum, declarat Iuuenalis his uersibus: nullum numen habes, si sit prudentia: nos te, nos facimus, fortuna, deam caeloque locamus.
passages.english:
And so, since they felt the force of this perverse power opposing virtue but did not know its name, they invented for themselves the empty word "fortune". How far this is removed from wisdom Juvenal declares in these verses:
You have no divinity, if there is prudence; it is we, we who make you, Fortune, a goddess and place you in heaven.

passages.original: stultitia igitur et error et caecitas pt, ut Cicero ait, ignoratio rerum atque causarum naturae ac fortunae nomina induxit.
passages.english: Folly, therefore, and error and blindness, and, as Cicero says, ignorance of things and causes, brought in the names of nature and fortune.
passages.notes: "pt" is apparently a scanning error, probably for "et"; translated as "and".

passages.original: deum uero esse patrem eundemque dominum utrique ignorauerunt, tam cultores deorum quam ipsi sapientiae professores, quia aut nihil omnino colendum putauerunt aut religiones falsas adprobauerunt aut, etiamsi uim potestatemque summi dei intellexerunt, ut Plato, qui ait unum esse fabricatorem mundi deum, et Marcus Tullius, qui fatetur hominem praeclara quadam condicione a supremo deo esse generatum, tamen ei debitum cultum tamquam summo patri non reddiderunt, quod erat consequens ac necessarium.
passages.english: But that God is the Father and likewise the Lord, both groups were ignorant, the worshippers of the gods as much as the professors of wisdom themselves, because they either thought nothing at all should be worshipped, or approved false religions, or, even if they understood the might and power of the supreme God, like Plato, who says that there is one God, the maker of the world, and Marcus Tullius, who admits that man was begotten by the supreme God in a certain glorious condition, nevertheless they did not render him the worship due to him as the highest Father, which was the consequent and necessary thing.

passages.original: et rursus in fine: ἄλλον ἔδωκε Θεὸς πιστοῖς ἀνδράσσι γεραίρειν. et alia Sibylla praecipit hunc oportere cognosci: αὐτὸν σου γίνωσκε Θεὸν Θεοῦ υἱὸν ἐόντα.
passages.english: And again at the end: "God gave another for faithful men to honour." And another Sibyl instructs that he must be known: "Know him as your God, being the Son of God."
passages.notes: Greek ἀνδράσσι read as ἀνδράσι; σου γίνωσκε probably for σὸν γίνωσκε.

passages.original: idcirco illum Trismegistus δημιουργὸν TOO seou et Sibylla σύμβουλον appellat, quod tanta sapientia et uirtute sit instructus a deo patre, ut consilio eius et manibus uteretur in fabricatione mundi.
passages.english: For this reason Trismegistus calls him the craftsman of God, and the Sibyl calls him counsellor, because he was furnished by God the Father with such wisdom and power that [God] used his counsel and his hands in the making of the world.
passages.notes: "TOO seou" is a scanning error for Greek τοῦ θεοῦ ("of God").

passages.original: uerum quoniam Graeci ueteres χρίεσθαι dicebant ungui, quod nunc ἀλείϕεσθαι, sicut indicat Homeri uersus ille: τοὺς δ\' ἐπεὶ οὖν δμῳαὶ λοῦσαν καὶ χρῖσαν ἐλαίῳ, ob hanc rationem nos eum Christum nuncupamus, id est unctum, qui Hebraeice Messias dicitur. unde in quibusdam Graecis scripturis, quae male de Hebraeicis interpretatae sunt, ήλειμ- μένος scriptum inuenitur, ἀπὸ tou ἀλείϕεσθαι.
passages.english: But since the ancient Greeks used chriesthai for being anointed, where they now say aleiphesthai, as that verse of Homer shows: "And when the maidservants had bathed them and anointed them with oil," for this reason we call him Christ, that is, anointed, who in Hebrew is called Messiah. Hence in certain Greek scriptures, which were badly translated from the Hebrew, ēleimmenos is found written, from aleiphesthai.
passages.notes: "tou" is a scanning error for Greek τοῦ; ήλειμ- μένος joined as ἠλειμμένος.

passages.original: deus autem cum solus adhuc esset, cui permiscere se potuit? aut cum esset tantae potestatis, ut quidquid uellet efficeret, utique ad creandum societate alterius non indigebat: nisi forte existimabimus deum, sicut Orpheus putauit, et marem esse et feminam, quod aliter generare non quiuerit, nisi haberet uim sexus utriusque, quasi aut ipse secum coierit aut sine coitu non potuerit procreare.
passages.english: But God, since he was as yet alone, with whom could he have mingled? Or, since he was of such great power that he could accomplish whatever he wished, he certainly did not need the partnership of another in order to create; unless perhaps we shall suppose, as Orpheus thought, that God is both male and female, because he could not otherwise have begotten unless he had the power of both sexes, as though either he had coupled with himself or could not have procreated without coupling.

passages.original: Ie-ssp autem fuit pater Dauid, ex cuius radice ascensurum esse florem praelocutus est, eum scilicet, de quo Sibylla dicit ἀνθήσει δ\' ἄνθος καθαρόν.
passages.english: Now Jesse was the father of David, from whose root he foretold that a flower would spring up, namely him of whom the Sibyl says: "A pure flower will blossom."
passages.notes: "Ie-ssp" is a scanning error for "Iesse" (Jesse).

passages.original: et haec omnia non manibus aut aliqua medella, sed uerbo ac iussione faciebat, sicut etiam Sibylla praedixerat: πάντα λόγῳ πράσσων πᾶσάν τε νόσον θεραπεύων
passages.english: And he did all these things not with his hands or with any remedy, but by word and command, just as the Sibyl had also foretold: "doing all things by a word, and healing every disease."

passages.original: sed et Sibylla eadem cecinit his uersibus:νεκρῶν δὲ ἀνάστασις ἔσται καὶ χωλῶν δρόμος ὠκύτατος καὶ κωφὸς ἀκούσει καὶ τυφλοὶ βλέψουσι, λαλήσουσ᾽ οὐ λαλέοντες. νεϰρω̃ν 8\' ὲπανάστασιςeatat xat xwXoivδρόμος ὼϰύτατος ϰαὶ ϰωϕόςaxoucet xat tuaXotβλέψουσι, λαλήσουσ\' OJ λαλέοντες.
passages.english: But the Sibyl too sang the same things in these verses: "There will be a resurrection of the dead, and the lame will run most swiftly, and the deaf will hear, and the blind will see, and those who do not speak will speak."
passages.notes: The Greek verses are printed twice; the second copy is a garbled scanning duplicate (reading ἐπανάστασις for ἀνάστασις) and has not been translated separately.

passages.original: idem hoc futurum etiam Sibylla contionata est: εἰς δὲ τὸ βρῶμα χολὴν καὶ εἰς δίψαν ὄξος ἔδωκαν,τῆς ἀφιλοξενίης ταύτην δείξουσι τράπεζαν. Et alia Sibylla Iudaeam terram his increpat increpat:
passages.english: The Sibyl also proclaimed that this same thing would happen: "And for food they gave gall, and for thirst vinegar; this is the table of inhospitality they will display." And another Sibyl rebukes the land of Judaea with these [verses]:
passages.notes: The final sentence is duplicated garbled text ("increpat increpat"); it anticipates the opening of the next passage.

passages.original: et alia Sibylla Iudaeam terram his increpat uersibus: αὐτὴ γὰρ δύσφρων, τὸν σὸν θεὸν οὐκ ἐνόησας παίζοντα θνητοῖσι νοήμασιν, ἀλλὰ ἀπ\' ἀκάνθης ἔστεψας στεφάνῳ φοβερὴν τε χολὴν ἐκέρασσας.
passages.english: And another Sibyl rebukes the land of Judaea with these verses: "For you yourself, perverse-minded, did not recognise your God, playing with mortal thoughts, but crowned [him] with a crown of thorns and mixed dreadful gall."
passages.notes: "Playing with mortal thoughts" (παίζοντα θνητοῖσι νοήμασιν) is obscure; it may mean God mocking the minds of mortals.

passages.original: item Hieremias: exterrita est quae parit et taeduit anima, et subiuit sol ei, cum adhuc medius dies esset, contusa est et maledicta: reliquos eorum in gladium dabo in conspectu inimicorum eorum. et Sibylla:
passages.english: Likewise Jeremiah: "She who gives birth is terrified, and her soul is weary, and the sun has gone down on her while it was still midday; she is bruised and cursed. The rest of them I will give to the sword in the sight of their enemies." And the Sibyl:
passages.notes: The passage ends at the introduction of a Sibylline quotation that is not included.

passages.original: et ideo Sibylla inpositurum esse morti terminum dixit post tridui somnum: καὶ θανάτου μοῖραν τελέσει τρίτον ἧμαρ ὑπνώσας·καὶ τότ᾽ ἀπὸ φθιμένων ἀναλύσας εἰς φάος ἥξει πρῶτος ἀναστάσεως κλητοῖς ἀρχὴν ὑποδείξας.
passages.english: And therefore the Sibyl said that he would set an end to death after a sleep of three days: "And he will fulfil the fate of death, having slept for the third day; and then, returning from the dead, he will come into the light, the first to show the called the beginning of resurrection."

passages.original: domum autem Iuda et Israhel non utique Iudaeos significat, quos abdicauit, sed nos, qui ab eo conuocati ex gentibus in illorum locum adoptione successimus et appellamur filii Iudaeorum: quod declarat Sibylla, cum dicit: Ἰουδαίων μακάρων θεῖον γένος οὐρανιώνων.
passages.english: But the house of Judah and Israel certainly does not signify the Jews, whom he has disowned, but us, who, called together by him out of the nations, have succeeded into their place by adoption and are called sons of the Jews. The Sibyl declares this when she says: "the divine, heavenly race of the blessed Jews."

passages.original: hoc uinculo pietatis obstricti deo et religati sumus: unde ipsa religio nomen accepit, non ut Cicero interpretatus est a relegendo, qui libro de natura deorum secundo ita dixit:
passages.english: By this bond of piety we are bound and tied back to God; from this religion itself received its name, not, as Cicero interpreted it, from "re-reading" (relegendo); he spoke thus in the second book On the Nature of the Gods:
passages.notes: Lactantius derives religio from religare ("to bind back"), against Cicero's derivation from relegere.

passages.original: eo melius ergo id nomen Lucretius interpretatus est, qui ait religionum se nodos soluere. superstitiosi autem uocantur non qui filios superstites optant — omnes enim optamus —, sed aut ii qui superstitem memoriam defunctorum colunt aut qui parentibus suis superstites colebant imagines eorum domi tamquam deos penates.
passages.english: So Lucretius interpreted that name better, when he says that he is loosing the knots of religions. But people are called superstitious not because they wish for their sons to survive them (for we all wish that), but either those who cultivate the surviving memory of the dead, or those who, having survived their parents, used to worship their images at home as household gods.
passages.notes: Lactantius derives religio from religare ('to bind') and superstitio from superstes ('surviving').

passages.original: eos uero qui publicos et antiquos deos colerent, religiosos nominabant. unde Vergilius: uana superstitio ueterumque ignara deorum.
passages.english: But those who worshipped the public and ancient gods they called religious. Hence Vergil: "empty superstition, ignorant of the ancient gods."

passages.original: et idcirco disceptatione sublata pellitur e medio sapientia, ui geritur res, ut ait Ennius. et quia student damnare tamquam nocentes quos utique sciunt innocentes, constare de ipsa innocentia nolunt: quasi uero maior iniquitas sit probatam innocentiam damnasse quam inauditam.
passages.english: And therefore, with debate removed, wisdom is driven out of the way, the matter is settled by force, as Ennius says. And because they are eager to condemn as guilty those whom they certainly know to be innocent, they do not want the innocence itself to be established: as if indeed it were a greater injustice to have condemned innocence once proved than [innocence] unheard.

passages.original: quis enim praesente ac uigente iustitia aut de tutela sui, cum nemo insidiaretur, aut de pernicie alterius cogitaret, cum nemo quicquam concupisceret? malebant tenui contenti uiuere cultu, ut Cicero in suo narrat: quod est proprium nostrae religionis. ne signare quidem aut partiri limite campum fas erat: in medium quaerebant,
passages.english: For while justice was present and flourishing, who would have thought either about protecting himself, when no one was plotting against him, or about the ruin of another, when no one desired anything? "They preferred to live content with slender means," as Cicero relates in his [work], which is proper to our religion. "It was not even right to mark out or divide the field with a boundary: they sought [their goods] for the common store,"
passages.notes: "ut Cicero in suo narrat" appears incomplete; the title of Cicero's work seems to have dropped out, and the verse quotations (Vergil, Georgics) may be misattributed or the text disturbed. The passage breaks off mid-quotation.

passages.original: quomodo laudem mereretur deuota deo suo fides, nisi esset aliquis qui a deo uellet auertere? nam ideo potentiores esse iniustos permisit, ut cogere ad malum possent, ideo plures, ut uirtus esset pretiosa, quod rara est. quod quidem ipsum Quintilianus egregie ac breuiter ostendit in Capite obuoluto.
passages.english: How would faithfulness devoted to its God earn praise, unless there were someone who wished to turn [it] away from God? For this reason he allowed the unjust to be more powerful, so that they could compel [people] to evil; and for this reason more numerous, so that virtue might be precious, because it is rare. Quintilian showed this very point excellently and briefly in The Muffled Head.
passages.notes: "Caput obuolutum" is the title of a declamation attributed to Quintilian.

passages.original: praeclare itaque M. Tullius: etenim si nemo est inquit quin emori malit quam conuerti in aliquam figuram bestiae, quamuis hominis mentem sit habiturus, quanto est miserius in hominis figura animo esse efferato? mihi quidem tanto uidetur, quanto praestabilior est animus corpore.
passages.english: So Marcus Tullius [puts it] splendidly: "For if there is no one," he says, "who would not rather die than be changed into some shape of a beast, even though he were to keep a human mind, how much more wretched is it to have a savage mind in a human shape? To me indeed it seems as much more wretched as the mind is superior to the body."

passages.original: est apud Ciceronem non abhorrens a uero locus in ea disputatione quae habetur a Furio contra iustitiam. quaero inquit, si duo sint, quorum alter. optimus uir, aequissimus, summa iustitia, singulari fide, alter insigni scelere et audacia, et si in eo sit errore ciuitas, ut bonum illum uirum sceleratum facinerosum nefarium putet, contra autem (eum) qui sit inprobis simus, elxistimet esse summa probitate ac fide, proque hac opinione omnium ciuium bonus ille uir uexetur rapiatur, manus ei denique auferantur, effodiantur oculi, damnetur uinciatur uratur exterminetur egeat,
passages.english: There is a passage in Cicero not far from the truth, in the debate that Furius conducts against justice. "I ask," he says, "if there were two men, of whom one was a most excellent man, most fair, of the highest justice and singular good faith, and the other of notable wickedness and audacity; and if the state were in such error that it thought that good man wicked, criminal, and abominable, and on the other hand judged the one who was most dishonest to be of the highest probity and good faith; and if, in accordance with this opinion of all the citizens, that good man were harassed, seized, finally had his hands cut off, his eyes gouged out, were condemned, bound, burned, banished, reduced to want,
passages.notes: Scanning errors read as 'improbissimus' and 'existimet'. The sentence breaks off unfinished.

passages.original: sua sibi habeant regna reges, suas diuitias diuites, ut loquitur Plautus, suam uero prudentiam prudentes: relinquant nobis stultitiam nostram, quam uel ex hoc apparet esse sapientiam quod eam nobis inuident.
passages.english: Let kings keep their kingdoms to themselves, the rich their riches, as Plautus says, and the prudent their prudence: let them leave us our folly, which is shown to be wisdom even from this, that they envy us it.

passages.original: recte igitur Seneca incongruentiam hominibus obiectans ait: summa uirtus illis uidetur magnus animus, et idem eum qui contemnit mortem pro furioso habent: quod est utique summae peruersitatis.
passages.english: Rightly, then, Seneca, reproaching people for their inconsistency, says: "The highest virtue in their eyes is a great spirit, and yet they consider the man who despises death a madman"; which is certainly the height of perversity.

passages.original: pietas uero et aequitas quasi uenae sunt eius, his enim duobus fontibus constat tota iustitia: sed caput eius et origo in illo primo est, in secundo uis omnis ac ratio. pietas autem nihil aliut est quam dei notio, sicut Trismegistus uerissime definiuit, ut alio loco diximus.
passages.english: Piety and equity are, as it were, its veins, for the whole of justice consists of these two springs; but its head and origin lie in the first, and all its force and method in the second. Piety is nothing other than the knowledge of God, as Trismegistus most truly defined it, as we have said elsewhere.

passages.original: altera est iustitiae pars aequitas: aequitatem dico non utique bene iudicandi, quod et ipsum laudabile est in homine iusto, sed se cum ceteris coaequandi, quam Cicero aequabilitatem uocat.
passages.english: The other part of justice is equity: I mean equity not, of course, in the sense of judging well, which is itself also praiseworthy in a just man, but of making oneself equal with others, which Cicero calls 'equability'.

passages.original: aput Ciceronem idem ille iustitiae defensor Laelius uult inquit paene uirtus honorem nec est uirtutis ulla alia merces. est plane et quidem uirtute dignissima, quam tu, Laeli, numquam poteras suspicari: nihil enim diuinarum noueras litterarum. quam tamen illa inquit accipit facile, exigit non acerbe. erras uehementer, si putas ab homine praemium solui posse uirtuti, cum ipse alio loco uerissime dixeris: huic tu uiro quas diuitias obicies?
passages.english: In Cicero that same defender of justice, Laelius, says: "Virtue all but wants honour, and there is no other reward for virtue." There plainly is [one], and indeed one most worthy of virtue, which you, Laelius, could never have suspected, for you knew nothing of the divine writings. "Yet she," he says, "accepts it readily and does not demand it harshly." You are badly mistaken if you think that a reward can be paid to virtue by a human being, since you yourself said most truly in another place: "What riches will you set before this man?
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-quotation; the context after continues it ("what commands? what kingdoms?").

passages.original: aput Ciceronem Catulus in Hortensio philosophiam rebus omnibus praeferens malle se dicit uel unum paruum de officio libellum quam longam orationem pro seditioso homine Cornelio. quae sententia non utique Catuli, qui illut fortasse non dixit, sed Ciceronis est putanda, qui scripsit, credo ut libros quos de officiis erat scripturus commendaret: in quibus ipsis nihil esse testatur in omni philosophia melius et fructuosius quam praecepta uitae dare.
passages.english: In Cicero, Catulus in the Hortensius, preferring philosophy to all things, says that he would rather have even one small little book on duty than a long speech on behalf of the seditious man Cornelius. This opinion is certainly to be regarded not as that of Catulus, who perhaps did not say it, but as that of Cicero, who wrote it, I believe, in order to recommend the books he was about to write on duties; in which very books he testifies that there is nothing in all philosophy better and more fruitful than giving precepts for life.

passages.original: breuius facere potuit, si tantum bonum ac malum diceret, quia nihil potest esse utile uel honestum quod non idem bonum sit, nihil inutile ac turpe quod non idem malum. quod et philosophis uidetur et idem Cicero in tertio supra dicti operis ostendit.
passages.english: He could have done it more briefly if he had said only good and evil, since nothing can be useful or honourable that is not also good, and nothing useless and base that is not also evil. This is the view of the philosophers too, and the same Cicero shows it in the third [book] of the work mentioned above.
passages.notes: The work referred to is presumably Cicero's On Duties (De officiis), Book 3.

passages.original: uerum est enim Ciceronis illut: qui autem ciuium rationem dicunt habendam, externorum negant, dirimunt hi communem humani generis societatem, qua sublata beneficentia liberalitas bonitas iustitia funditus tollitur.
passages.english: For that saying of Cicero is true: "But those who say that account must be taken of citizens but deny it of foreigners, these break apart the common fellowship of the human race; and when that is removed, beneficence, generosity, goodness and justice are utterly destroyed."

passages.original: itaque non errat Lucretius, cum dicit: denique caelesti sumus omnes semine oriundi,omnibus ille idem pater est.
passages.english: And so Lucretius is not mistaken when he says: "In short, we are all sprung from heavenly seed; / all have that same father."

passages.original: -discordia igitur ac dissensio non est secundum hominis rationem uerumque illut est Ciceronis, quod ait hominem naturae oboedientem homini nocere non posse. ergo si nocere homini contra naturam est, prodesse igitur homini secundum naturam sit necesse est.
passages.english: Discord, then, and dissension are not in accordance with man's reason, and that saying of Cicero is true, where he says that a man who obeys nature cannot harm a man. Therefore, if harming a man is contrary to nature, then helping a man must necessarily be in accordance with nature.

passages.original: praecipua igitur uirtus hospitalitas, quod philosophi quoque aiunt, sed eam detorquent a uera iustitia et ad commodum rapiunt. recte inquit Cicero a Theophrasto est laudata hospitalitas. est enim, ut mihi quidem uidetur, ualde decorum patere domus hominum inlustrium hospitibus inlustribus.
passages.english: Hospitality, then, is a chief virtue, as the philosophers also say, but they twist it away from true justice and drag it toward advantage. "Rightly," says Cicero, "was hospitality praised by Theophrastus. For it is, as it seems to me at least, very fitting that the houses of distinguished men should be open to distinguished guests."

passages.original: atquin ego non arguta aliqua conclusione, ut aput Platonem Socrates facit, qui eos quos contra disputat cogit ea quae negauerant confiteri, sed simpliciter ostendam summum metum summam esse uirtutem.
passages.english: And yet I will not [do this] by some clever syllogism, as Socrates does in Plato, who compels those against whom he argues to admit the things they had denied; rather, I will show plainly that the greatest fear is the greatest virtue.
passages.notes: "aput" is a variant spelling of "apud". "conclusione" here means a logical conclusion or syllogism.

passages.original: uera igitur Ciceronis illa sententia est: nemo inquit iustus potest esse qui mortem, qui dolorem, qui exsilium, qui egestatem timet;
passages.english: True, then, is that opinion of Cicero: "No one," he says, "can be just who fears death, pain, exile, or poverty;"

passages.original: duobus igitur uerbis duas uirtutes maximas bono et sapienti uiro, innocentiam patientiamque, detraxit. sed quia ipse caninam illam facundiam, sicut Sallustius ab Appio dictum refert, exercuit, uoluit hominem canino modo uiuere, ut remordeat lacessitus.
passages.english: With two words, then, he stripped the good and wise man of two very great virtues, innocence and patience. But because he himself practised that "dog-like eloquence," as Sallust reports it was called by Appius, he wanted a man to live in dog-like fashion, so that when provoked he bites back.
passages.notes: The subject ("he") is not identified within the passage; from Lactantius' argument it is probably Cicero.

passages.original: Cicero in Catone maiore stupra uero inquit et adulteria et omne flagitium nullis excitari aliis inlecebris nisi uoluptatis. cumque homini siue natura siue quis deus nihil mente praestabilius dedisset, huic diuino muneri ac dono nihil tam inimicum quam uoluptatem:
passages.english: Cicero in the Cato Maior [says]: "Debaucheries, indeed, and adulteries and every disgraceful act are stirred up by no other enticements than those of pleasure.
