And since nature or some god had given man nothing more excellent than the mind, to this divine gift and present nothing is so hostile as pleasure."

passages.original: itaque m aram dei, quae uere maxima est et quae in corde hominis conlocata inquinari non potest sanguine, iustitia imponitur, patientia fides innocentia castitas abstinentia. hic est uerissimus ritus, haec illa lex dei, ut a Cicerone dictum est, praeclara et diuina, semper quae recta et honesta iubet, uetat praua et turpia: cui parentem sanctissimae ac certissimae legi iuste ac legitime necesse est uiuere.
passages.english: Therefore on the altar of God, which is truly the greatest and which, set in the heart of man, cannot be defiled with blood, justice is laid, [and] patience, faith, innocence, chastity, abstinence. This is the truest rite, this is that law of God, as Cicero said, excellent and divine, which always commands what is right and honourable [and] forbids what is wicked and base: obeying this most holy and most certain law, one must live justly and lawfully.
passages.notes: The stray 'm' before 'aram' is taken as a footnote mark and omitted.

passages.original: quanto melius et uerius Seneca uultisne uos inquit deum cogitare magnum et placidum et maiestate leni uerendum, amicum et semper in proximo, non immo lationibus nec sanguine multo colendum — quae enim ei trucidatione immerentium uoluptas est? —, sed mente pura, bono honestoque proposito?
passages.english: How much better and more truly Seneca [says]: "Do you wish," he says, "to think of God as great and peaceful and to be revered for his gentle majesty, a friend and always close at hand, to be worshipped not with sacrifices and much blood (for what pleasure does he have in the slaughter of the innocent?) but with a pure mind, with a good and honourable purpose?"
passages.notes: 'immo lationibus' read as 'immolationibus' (sacrifices).

passages.original: ita fit ut natum sit quidquid potest interire. sed et omne quod sub uisum oculorum uenit, et corporale, ut ait so Plato, et solubile sit necesse est.
passages.english: So it follows that whatever can perish was born. But also everything that comes under the sight of the eyes must, as Plato says, be both bodily and dissoluble.
passages.notes: The stray 'so' before 'Plato' is taken as a scanning error or marginal mark and omitted.

passages.original: unus igitur Epicurus auctore Democrito ueridicus in hac re fuit, qui ait et ortum aliquando et aliquando esse periturum. nec tamen rationem reddere ullam potuit aut quibus de causis tantum hoc opus aut quo tempore resoluatur.
passages.english: Epicurus alone, therefore, following Democritus, spoke the truth in this matter, saying that [the world] both arose at some time and will at some time perish. And yet he could give no account either of the causes for which so great a work is dissolved or of the time when.

passages.original: reddant ergo isti rationem, si possunt, cur aut factus in principio sit aut postea resoluatur. quod quia docere non poterat Epicurus siue Democritus, sua sponte natum esse dixit seminibus inter se passim coeuntibus: quibus iterum resolutis discidium atque interitum secuturum.
passages.english: Let them therefore give an account, if they can, of why [the world] was either made in the beginning or is afterwards dissolved. Because Epicurus, or Democritus, could not teach this, he said that it was born of its own accord, from seeds coming together at random with one another, and that when these were dissolved again, separation and destruction would follow.

passages.original: respondendum est hoc loco philosophis maximeque Ciceroni, qui ait: cur deus omnia nostra causa cum faceret, tantam uim natricum uiperarumque fe-\' cerit? cur tam multa pestifera terra marique disperserit?
passages.english: At this point we must answer the philosophers, and above all Cicero, who says: "Why, when God made all things for our sake, did he make such a multitude of water-snakes and vipers? Why did he scatter so many pestilent things over land and sea?"
passages.notes: 'fe-\' cerit' read as 'fecerit'.

passages.original: quae utilitas deo in homine, inquit Epicurus ut eum propter se faceret? scilicet ut esset qui opera eius intellegeret, qui prouidentiam disponendi, rationem faciendi, uirtutem consummandi et sensu admirari et uoce proloqui posset: quorum omnium summa haec est, ut deum colat.
passages.english: "What use was man to God," says Epicurus, "that he should make him for his own sake?" Clearly, that there might be someone who would understand his works, who could both admire with his senses and declare with his voice the providence of his ordering, the reason of his making, the power of his completing: and the sum of all these is this, that he should worship God.

passages.original: ob has eorum pertinacissimas contentiones nulla extitit philosophia quae ad uerum propius accederet: nam particulatim ueritas ab iis tota conprehensa est. factum esse a deo mundum dixit Plato:
passages.english: Because of these most obstinate disputes of theirs, no philosophy arose that came nearer to the truth; for the truth was grasped by them in its entirety [only] piecemeal. Plato said that the world was made by God:
passages.notes: The passage ends with a colon introducing a quotation not included here.

passages.original: haec fere Platonis collecta breuiter, quae aput ipsum late copioseque explicantur. in eadem sententia fuit etiam Pythagoras antea eiusque praeceptor Pherecydes, quem Cicero tradidit primum de aeternitate animarum disputauisse.
passages.english: These are, roughly, the views of Plato briefly collected, which are set out at length and in abundance in his own work. Of the same opinion was also Pythagoras before him, and his teacher Pherecydes, who, Cicero records, was the first to argue about the eternity of souls.

passages.original: opera corporis atque animi nonne indicant esse animam mortis expertem? nam corpus quia ipsum fragile est atque mortale, quaecumque opera molitur, aeque caduca sunt. nihil enim Tullius ait esse quod sit manibus humanis laboratum, quod non aliquando ad interitum redigatur uel iniuria hominum uel ipsa confectrice rerum omnium uetustate.
passages.english: Do not the works of body and of mind show that the soul is exempt from death? For the body, because it is itself fragile and mortal, whatever works it toils at are equally perishable. For nothing, Tullius says, is wrought by human hands that is not at some time brought to destruction, either by the injury of men or by age itself, the consumer of all things.

passages.original: solidum enim et conprehensibile corpus est et oculis et manu, anima uero tenuis et tactum uisumque fugiens. corpus e terra fictum atque solidatum est, anima nihil in se concreti, nihil ponderis terreni habet, ut Plato disserebat. nec enim tantam posset habere sollertiam, tantam uim, tantam celeritatem, nisi originem traheret e caelo.
passages.english: For the body is solid and can be grasped both by the eyes and by the hand, but the soul is fine and escapes touch and sight. The body has been fashioned from earth and made solid; the soul has nothing compacted in it, nothing of earthly weight, as Plato used to argue. For it could not have such skill, such power, such swiftness, unless it drew its origin from heaven.

passages.original: Plato et multi alii philosophorum cum ignorarent originem rerum supremumque illut tempus quo mundus esset effectus, multa milia saeculorum fluxisse dixerunt, ex quo hic pulcherrimus mundi extiterit ornatus, secuti fortasse Chaldaeos, qui, ut Cicero tradit in libro de diuinatione primo, quadringenta septuaginta milia annorum monumentis conprehensa se habere delirant: in quo se quia posse argui non putabant, liberum sibi crediderunt esse mentiri.
passages.english: Plato and many others of the philosophers, since they did not know the origin of things and that first moment at which the world was made, said that many thousands of ages had passed since this most beautiful ordering of the world came into being. In this they perhaps followed the Chaldaeans, who, as Cicero relates in the first book On Divination, rave that they possess four hundred and seventy thousand years recorded in their monuments. Because they thought they could not be refuted in this, they believed they were free to lie.

passages.original: et tamen idem testati sunt non auctorem se certum, sed opinionem sequi, ut Maro qui ait: sit mihi fas audita loqui.
passages.english: And yet the same men have testified that they follow not a certain authority but opinion, like Maro, who says: "May it be lawful for me to tell what I have heard."
passages.notes: Maro is Virgil; the quotation is Aeneid 6.266.

passages.original: unde Vergilius: o pater, anne aliquas ad caelum hinc ire putandum est sublimis animas iterumque ad tarda reuerti corpora? quae lucis miseris tam dira cupido?
passages.english: Hence Virgil: "O father, must we think that some souls go from here up to the sky, exalted, and return again to sluggish bodies? What so dreadful longing for the light do the wretched have?"

passages.original: unde etiam Plato de anima disserens ex hoc ait posse cognosci animas esse inmortales atque diuinas, quod in pueris mobilia sint ingenia et ad percipiendum facilia, quod ea quae discant ita celeriter rapiant, ut non tunc primum discere illa uideantur, sed recognoscere atque reminisci: in quo uir sapiens poetis ineptissime credidit.
passages.english: Hence also Plato, discussing the soul, says that it can be known that souls are immortal and divine from this: that in children the intellect is quick and ready to learn, and that they seize what they learn so swiftly that they seem not to be learning those things for the first time but to be recognising and recalling them. In this the wise man most foolishly believed the poets.

passages.original: meiius Chrysippus, quem Cicero ait fulcire porticum Stoicorum: qui in libris quos de prouidentia scripsit cum de innouatione mundi loqueretur, haec intulit: τούτου δέ οὕτως ἔχοντος δῆλον, ὡς οὐδὲν ἀδύνατον, καὶ ἡμᾶς μετά τὸ τελευτῆσαι πάλιν περιόδῳ τινὶ χρόνου εἰς τοῦτο ἐν ᾧ νῦν ἐσμεν ἀποκαταστῆναι σχῆμα.
passages.english: Better [was] Chrysippus, who, Cicero says, props up the Porch of the Stoics. In the books he wrote On Providence, when speaking of the renewal of the world, he added this: "This being so, it is clear that nothing is impossible, and that we too, after we have died, after some period of time, will be restored again to this shape in which we now are."
passages.notes: 'meiius' is a scanning error for 'melius'.

passages.original: sed nos ab humanis ad diuina redeamus. Sibylla dicit haec: δύσπιστον γὰρ ἅπαν μερόπων γένος. ἀλλ᾽ ὅταν ἠδὴ κόσμου καὶ θνητῶν ἔλθῃ κρίσις, ἣν θεὸς αὐτὸς ποιήσει κρίνων ἀσεβεῖς θ᾽ ἅμα εὐσεβέας τε,καὶ τότε δυσσεβέας μὲν ἐπὶ ζόφον ἐν πυρὶ πέμψει. ὅσσοι δ᾽ εὐσεβέουσι, πάλιν ζήσουσ᾽ ἐπὶ γαίης,πνεῦμα θεοῦ δόντος τιμὴν ἅμα καὶ βίον αὐτοῖς.
passages.english: But let us return from human to divine things. The Sibyl says this: "For the whole race of mortals is slow to believe. But when at last the judgement of the world and of mortals comes, which God himself will make, judging the impious and the pious together, then he will send the ungodly into darkness in fire; but all who are pious will live again upon the earth, God giving them breath, and honour and life together."

passages.original: Nunc reliqua subnectam. ueniet igitur summi et maximi dei filius, ut uiuos ac mortuos iudicet, Sibylla testante atque dicente: , πάσης γὰρ γαίης τότε θνητῶν σύγχυσις ἔσται,αὐτὸς ὁ παντοκράτωρ ὅταν ἐλθῃ βήματι κρῖναι ζώντων καὶ νεκύων ψυχὰς καὶ κόσμον ἅπαντα.
passages.english: Now I will append the rest. The Son of the highest and greatest God, then, will come to judge the living and the dead, as the Sibyl testifies and says: "For then there will be confusion of mortals over all the earth, when the Almighty himself comes to his judgement seat to judge the souls of the living and the dead, and the whole world."
passages.notes: A stray comma before the Greek quotation has been ignored.

passages.original: post cuius aduentum congregabuntur iusti ex omni terra peractoque iudicio ciuitas sancta constituetur in medio terrae, in qua ipse conditor deus cum iustis dominantibus commoretur. quam ciuitatem Sibylla designat, cum dicit: καὶ πόλιν, ἥν ἐπόθησε θεὸς, ταύτην ἐποίησεν λαμπροτέραν ἄστρων ἠδ\' ἡλίου ἠδὲ σελήνης.
passages.english: After his coming the righteous will be gathered from all the earth, and when the judgement has been completed a holy city will be established in the middle of the earth, in which God the founder himself will dwell together with the righteous, who will rule. This city the Sibyl indicates when she says: "And the city which God desired, this he made brighter than the stars and the sun and the moon."

passages.original: at uero cum caput illut orbis occiderit et ῥύμη esse coeperit, quod Sibyllae fore aiunt, quis dubitet uenisse iam finem rebus humanis orbique terrarum?
passages.english: But when that head of the world has fallen and has begun to be a *rhymē* [street], as they say the Sibyls [declare] will happen, who could doubt that the end has already come for human affairs and the whole world?
passages.notes: Greek ῥύμη ('street', 'lane') is a pun on Rome (Ῥώμη): Rome will be reduced to a mere street. Some editions read the phrase with ῥύμη in place of a city name.

passages.original: hunc sequamur omnes, hunc audiamus, huic deuotissime pareamus, quoniam solus, ut ait Lucretius, ueridicis hominum purgauit pectora dictis et finem statuit cuppedinis atque timoris exposuitque bonum summum, quo tendimus omnes, quid foret, atque uiam monstrauit, limite paruo qua possemus ad id recto contendere cursu.
passages.english: Let us all follow him, let us listen to him, let us obey him most devotedly, since he alone, as Lucretius says, "cleansed the hearts of men with truth-telling words, and set a limit to desire and fear, and set forth what the highest good was, toward which we all strive, and showed the way by which, along a narrow path, we might press on to it in a straight course."
passages.notes: The quoted lines are Lucretius, De rerum natura 6.24–28, where they praise Epicurus; Lactantius here applies them to Christ. 'Cuppedinis' (desire) is the archaic form used in Lucretius.
